title: Ind AS 113 "Fair Value Measurement"
outcomes: Explain the exit-price definition of fair value.
Identify the principal or most advantageous market and treat costs.
Apply highest and best use for non-financial assets.
Choose valuation techniques and classify measurements in the hierarchy.

meta.exam_tip: In market questions, compute net amounts only to pick the market; then price less transport only.

concepts.title: Definition of fair value and market participants
body: Fair value means the amount that market participants would pay you for an asset, or that you would pay them to take over a liability, in a normal (orderly) deal on the measurement date — an exit price, market-based rather than entity-specific.

The measurement reflects characteristics of the asset or liability (condition, location, restrictions that would transfer to a buyer) and the unit of account set by other standards. An orderly transaction assumes usual marketing activities, not a forced sale.
Market participants are independent, knowledgeable, able and willing buyers and sellers; fair value uses the assumptions they would use in pricing, assuming they act in their economic best interest.

Ind AS 113 explains how to measure fair value when another standard requires or permits it; it does not decide when fair value is used. Some measurements (e.g. share-based payments, leases, value in use, net realisable value) are outside its scope.
concepts.analogy: Fair value asks what the market would pay to buy it from you today — not what it is worth to you.
concepts.work: A restriction on selling shares that would pass to a buyer reduces fair value; one personal to the holder does not.

concepts.title: Principal and most advantageous market; costs
body: Fair value is measured assuming the transaction takes place in the principal market (where the asset trades most often and in the largest quantities) or, in its absence, the most advantageous market (maximising the amount received after transaction and transport costs).
The price in that market is not adjusted for transaction costs (they belong to the transaction, not the asset), but is adjusted for transport costs if location is a characteristic of the asset.
Transaction costs are used only to identify the most advantageous market. The entity must have access to the market at the measurement date, though it need not be able to sell on that date.
concepts.analogy: Choose the market first, then use its price less only the cost of getting the asset there.
concepts.work: Fresh produce valued at the city wholesale market price less transport from the farm.

concepts.title: Non-financial assets: highest and best use
body: For non-financial assets, fair value looks at how a market participant could earn the most from the asset — either through its own highest and best use or through a sale to a buyer who would use it that way.

Highest and best use must be physically possible, legally permissible and financially feasible. It is determined from market participants' perspective, even if the entity intends a different use; current use is presumed highest and best unless market factors suggest otherwise.
The valuation premise may be stand-alone or in combination with other assets and liabilities.
concepts.analogy: Value a non-financial asset as the market would best use it, not as the owner happens to use it.
concepts.work: A building used as a warehouse in a prime retail zone may be valued as shop space.

concepts.title: Valuation techniques and the fair value hierarchy
body: Valuation techniques: market approach (prices and information from market transactions in identical or comparable items), cost approach (current replacement cost adjusted for obsolescence), and income approach (discounting future cash flows or earnings, e.g. present value or option pricing). Techniques maximise relevant observable inputs and minimise unobservable inputs.

Fair value hierarchy: Level 1 — quoted prices in active markets for identical items at the measurement date; Level 2 — inputs other than Level 1 that are observable directly or indirectly (quoted prices for similar items, interest rates, yield curves); Level 3 — unobservable inputs based on the best available information, including the entity's own data adjusted to market participants' assumptions. The level is set by the lowest level input significant to the whole measurement.

Liabilities and own equity instruments are measured assuming transfer to a market participant, reflecting non-performance risk (including own credit). When fair value at initial recognition differs from transaction price, the difference is recognised in profit or loss only if supported by Level 1 or Level 2 evidence; otherwise it is deferred. Disclosures are more extensive for Level 3 measurements.
concepts.analogy: The more a value relies on observable market data, the higher its place in the hierarchy.
concepts.work: An unlisted equity valued on a discounted cash flow model with internal forecasts is Level 3.

illustrations.title: Which market sets the price?
illustrations.q: A commodity can be sold in Market A at ₹48 (transaction cost ₹4, transport cost ₹3) or Market B at ₹46 (transaction cost ₹1, transport cost ₹3). (a) There is no principal market. (b) Market A is the principal market. Determine fair value in each case.

head: Case
Fair value
Reason
rows: B gives the higher net amount; fair value is B's price less transport only
Principal market price less transport; transaction costs are not deducted
solution.title: Fair value

checks.label: Net amount receivable in Market A
Net amount receivable in Market B
Fair value if B is the most advantageous market
Fair value if A is the principal market

illustrations.title: Land used as a factory
illustrations.q: An entity acquires land in a business combination; it is used as a factory site worth ₹60 crore in that use. Nearby land has been rezoned for housing and the plot could be sold for residential development for ₹90 crore after demolition and rezoning costs of ₹12 crore. Development is physically possible, legally permissible and financially feasible. What is the fair value?

head: Use
Value ₹ crore
rows: Residential use, net of conversion costs
solution.title: Highest and best use

solution.text: Fair value is ₹78 crore — the highest and best use from a market participant's view — even though the entity intends to keep running the factory.

checks.label: Value as residential land net of conversion costs (₹ crore)

jobs.title: Review of a valuation report
jobs.situation: A client measures investment property and unlisted shares at fair value using an external valuer.
steps: Check the market and highest-and-best-use assumptions.
Identify the valuation technique and inputs.
Assign hierarchy levels based on significant inputs.
jobs.takeaway: Fair value audits focus on inputs and their observability, not just the final number.

mcqs.q: Fair value under Ind AS 113 is:
mcqs.explain: It is the price received to sell or paid to transfer. In practice: entity-specific values are excluded.
mcqs.topic: Definition of fair value and market participants

mcqs.q: When measuring fair value, transaction costs are:
options: Not deducted from the price, but used to identify the most advantageous market
mcqs.explain: They are characteristics of the transaction, not the asset. In practice: transport costs are deducted if location matters.
mcqs.topic: Principal and most advantageous market; costs

mcqs.q: The principal market is the market with:
options: The largest trading volume and activity for that asset
mcqs.explain: If a principal market exists, it is used even if another offers a better price. In practice: presumed to be the usual market.
mcqs.topic: Principal and most advantageous market; costs

mcqs.q: Highest and best use must be:
options: Physically possible, legally permissible and financially feasible
The use giving the highest accounting profit
mcqs.explain: All three tests apply from a market participant's view. In practice: current use is presumed unless evidence suggests otherwise.
mcqs.topic: Non-financial assets: highest and best use

mcqs.q: Quoted prices for similar assets in active markets are:
mcqs.explain: Level 1 needs identical items; similar items are Level 2. In practice: adjustments may move it to Level 3.
mcqs.topic: Valuation techniques and the fair value hierarchy

mcqs.q: A measurement's hierarchy level is determined by:
options: The lowest level input significant to the entire measurement
mcqs.explain: One significant unobservable input makes the measurement Level 3. In practice: assess significance carefully.
mcqs.topic: Valuation techniques and the fair value hierarchy

options: The current replacement cost adjusted for obsolescence
mcqs.explain: It reflects what it would cost to replace the service capacity. In practice: used for specialised assets.
mcqs.topic: Valuation techniques and the fair value hierarchy

mcqs.q: Fair value of a liability reflects:
options: Non-performance risk, including the entity's own credit risk
The amount the entity intends to pay
mcqs.explain: Liabilities are measured as if transferred to a market participant. In practice: own credit affects value.
mcqs.topic: Valuation techniques and the fair value hierarchy

summary: Exit price; orderly transaction; market participants.
Transaction costs not deducted; transport costs deducted if location matters.
HBU: physically possible, legally permissible, financially feasible.
remember: Lowest significant input sets the level.
traps: Intended use does not override highest and best use.

viva.q: Why is fair value called a market-based measure?
viva.model: Because it uses the assumptions market participants would use in pricing, not the entity's own intentions or value in use.
If location is a characteristic of the asset, the price in the principal or most advantageous market is adjusted for the cost of transporting it there.

viva.q: What is highest and best use?
viva.model: The use of a non-financial asset by market participants that maximises its value, being physically possible, legally permissible and financially feasible.
The market approach, the cost approach and the income approach.
Unobservable inputs reflecting the best available information, including the entity's own data adjusted to what market participants would assume.

cases.title: Horizon Investments Ltd.
cases.case: Horizon Investments Ltd. holds: (i) shares of a company listed on NSE, actively traded; (ii) corporate bonds valued using yields of similar bonds; (iii) shares of an unlisted start-up valued by a DCF model using management's forecasts; (iv) a building used as its office in an area where hotels pay much higher prices for similar buildings.

mcqs.explain: Quoted price for identical shares in an active market. In practice: price × quantity, no blockage discount.
mcqs.topic: Valuation techniques and the fair value hierarchy

mcqs.explain: Observable yields on similar instruments are Level 2 inputs. In practice: check comparability.
mcqs.topic: Valuation techniques and the fair value hierarchy

mcqs.explain: Management forecasts are unobservable inputs significant to the value. In practice: extensive disclosures.
mcqs.topic: Valuation techniques and the fair value hierarchy

options: Highest and best use, possibly as a hotel if feasible
mcqs.explain: Market participant view decides the use if physically, legally and financially feasible. In practice: disclose if use differs.
mcqs.topic: Non-financial assets: highest and best use
